strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: The Cauchy factorization of the GFT (Theorem 3.1) is original, rigorously proven, and generalizes prior work to arbitrary hierarchical graphs. Treatment of edge cases (repeated eigenvalues, orthogonal updates) is careful and thorough.

Rigorous algorithmic design and analysis: Theorem 3.2 provides formal O(n²k) complexity characterization with clear dependence on interface size. Greedy HGF construction and interface sparsification with theoretical guarantees (Theorem 4.1) demonstrate thoughtful algorithm engineering.

Compelling synthetic validation: Figures 2-3 convincingly demonstrate predicted O(n²k) and O(k) scaling laws, with negligible preprocessing overhead. Theory-practice alignment on controlled synthetic graphs is excellent.

Parameter efficiency and interpretability: Achieves competitive performance with orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters than transformer baselines. Grad-CAM analysis (Figure 5) provides intuitive evidence of localized spectral processing.
Strong mathematical exposition: Comprehensive proofs, careful notation, effective use of appendices. Core theoretical ideas are clearly motivated and well-developed.
weaknesses: Marginal empirical improvements with large error bars: Real-world performance gains over Stable-ChebNet are within or overlap standard deviations on 3/4 datasets (Roman-Empire: 92.12±1.12 vs 92.03±0.85; Amazon-Ratings: 53.41±1.3 vs 53.15±0.2; Tolokers: 85.57±0.61 vs 85.55±3.34). Only Minesweeper shows clear improvement. With only 4 datasets from a single benchmark, practical impact is unclear.

Critical theory-practice gap on complexity: Quadratic complexity O(n²k) requires small interface size k=O(1). For general graphs, k can be O(n), reverting to O(n³). Tolokers—explicitly called a 'worst-case scenario'—has k=25 after aggressive sparsification, yet is presented as a success. No characterization of when favorable hierarchical structure occurs in practice.

Unquantified approximation error propagation: Theorem 4.1 guarantees (1±ε)-spectral equivalence but ε is never specified for tested datasets. The claim that O(ε·L)-bounded output deviation holds for Lipschitz filters appears after Theorem 4.1 without empirical validation. Impact of 99.5% edge sparsification on spectral properties not studied. No ablation on sparsification ratio.

Extensive dataset-specific hyperparameter tuning without principled guidance: Table 3 reveals dramatic variation (Layers: 3-14, K: 4-8, Banks vary, Dropout: 0.2-0.3, Sparsification: 0.005-0.01). No ablation studies justifying these choices. No clear procedure for practitioners to set hyperparameters on new datasets. Unclear whether improvements stem from method or careful tuning.

Limited experimental scope: Only 4 datasets from single benchmark (Platonov et al., 2023). All transductive despite claiming inductive compatibility—no inductive experiments. Graphs are small (10K-24K nodes); no large-scale experiments where O(n²) savings would be most impactful. Missing comparisons with other spectral methods beyond Stable-ChebNet and Global GFT.

Incremental architectural contribution: Section 5 applies the factorization straightforwardly with standard learnable filters. ODE-inspired formulation (Eq. 18-19) relegated to appendix and feels disconnected. No ablation studies on number of hierarchy levels L, number of filter banks, or filter parameterization choices. Why this specific architecture?

Unsubstantiated theoretical claims: Connection between spectral locality (Definition A, appendix) and practical node-domain locality not rigorously established. Claims about avoiding oversquashing lack formal justification. Figure 5's localization interpretation is suggestive but not rigorous.

Presentation and reproducibility gaps: Important details scattered across appendices (ODE formulation B.1, learnable filters B.2, deflation C). Unclear when to use L2G-Net versus alternatives—only vague guidance ('when long-range dependencies essential'). No discussion of failure modes. Inconsistent use of normalized vs. combinatorial Laplacian. No code provided.

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: Theorem 3.1 elegantly generalizes Cauchy factorization from path graphs to arbitrary hierarchical graph families; Theorem 3.2 establishes clear O(n²k) complexity with thorough proofs
Synthetic experiments convincingly validate theoretical predictions: Figures 2-3 demonstrate predicted O(kn²) scaling and O(k) linear scaling with interface size, confirming theory-practice alignment
Well-motivated problem articulation: Clear identification of fundamental trade-off between global spectral methods (expensive O(n³)) and local message-passing (efficient but limited receptive field)

Rigorous mathematical treatment: Careful handling of edge cases including repeated eigenvalues via deflation (Section C), spectral sparsification with formal guarantees (Theorem 4.1), and detailed algorithmic descriptions
Interpretability analysis demonstrates principled locality-globality trade-off: Grad-CAM study (Figure 5) shows L2G-Net concentrates attributions on smaller node subsets compared to fully global GFT
weaknesses: Limited empirical superiority on real-world benchmarks: Underperforms state-of-the-art on 3/4 test datasets (Roman-Empire: 92.12 vs Polynormer 92.55; Amazon-Ratings: 53.41 vs 54.81; Tolokers: 85.57 vs 85.91)

Modest practical speedups limited to preprocessing: Table 2 shows only 2-3× speedup on preprocessing while eigendecomposition is computed once; no end-to-end training time comparisons provided, limiting practical impact

Questionable alignment with real-world graph properties: Benchmarks designed for non-local dependencies not necessarily hierarchical structure; aggressive sparsification required (k=25 vs original degree 88), suggesting artificial hierarchy

Specialized applicability significantly limits scope: Method efficiency critically depends on finding hierarchical decompositions with small interface sizes; applicability unclear for graphs without natural modular structure; no evaluation on graphs with strong hierarchical properties

Limited experimental scope: Single benchmark suite with 4 datasets; missing comparisons with other fast spectral methods (Givens rotations, butterfly factorizations); no ablations on sparsification ratio impact

Unclear when to adopt over alternatives: Paper acknowledges specialization to hierarchical structures but provides limited guidance on detecting/exploiting such structure; no analysis of what fraction of real-world graphs benefit

Hyperparameter sensitivity not addressed: Table 3 shows large variance in dataset-specific settings (layers: 3-14, filter banks: 1-6, sparsification: 0.005-0.01); hyperparameter selection process not explained
Theoretical limitations underexplored: Conditions for efficiency (small k) not formally characterized for real graphs; worst-case complexity remains O(n³) when k→O(n)

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: Rigorous generalization of Cauchy factorization from path graphs to arbitrary symmetric matrices, with sound complexity analysis (O(kn²)) validated experimentally on synthetic graphs
Novel architecture design: L2G-Net's principle of inserting learnable filters between hierarchical Cauchy factors represents a genuine contribution combining local and global spectral processing

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Covers synthetic validation, transductive heterophilous benchmarks, inductive long-range tasks, and large-scale graphs (569k nodes); demonstrates scalability where full eigendecomposition fails
Parameter efficiency: Orders of magnitude fewer learnable parameters than transformer baselines (Figure 5) while maintaining competitive accuracy—a meaningful practical advantage
Thorough presentation: Extensive supplementary materials with complete proofs, detailed algorithms, and careful treatment of edge cases (deflation, near-degenerate eigenvalues)
Interpretability: Learned filters show task-adaptive frequency responses (Figure 9) and node-level attribution is more localized than global spectral or attention methods (Figure 6)
weaknesses: Limited practical speedup: Per-epoch cost is O(n²), making L2G-Net 2-20× slower than GCN/ChebNet (Table 11); wall-clock advantage only from faster convergence, not algorithmic efficiency (Table 10)

Inconsistent and modest empirical results: Often competitive but rarely clearly superior—Minesweeper within std dev of Polynormer (97.50 vs 97.46), Roman-empire lags (92.12 vs 92.55); performance improvements frequently within error margins

Narrow target regime with unclear applicability: Method requires hierarchical graph structure (k ≪ n) and preference for spectral processing; paper does not characterize what fraction of real-world graphs satisfy these conditions or provide guidance on when to use L2G-Net vs. alternatives

Missing critical ablations: No analysis of sensitivity to hierarchy depth L, sparsification ratio ρ, or comparison of greedy partitioning to alternative methods (METIS, recursive bisection); design choices in Table 8 appear arbitrary without justification

Unanalyzed approximation error propagation: Spectral sparsification introduces error ε (Theorem 4.1), but empirical impact on GNN performance across multiple layers is not validated; theoretical guarantees and practical degradation may diverge
Partition quality heuristic without guarantees: Greedy HGF construction lacks optimality guarantees; no comparison to optimal or alternative partitions for the same graphs
Large error bars in results: Several benchmarks (Table 2 Roman-empire: ±1.1%, Table 7 London: 55.6±0.6) have overlapping confidence intervals, weakening conclusions about superiority
Limited benchmark diversity: Focuses on heterophilous and long-range regimes (specialized); omits standard homophilic benchmarks (Cora, Citeseer, OGB), limiting assessment of general applicability
